Title: Kenyan adults face high post-traumatic stress disorder risk: Study reveals patterns
NewsSummary: Genetic research shapes mental health care
NewsContent:
​A new study has revealed that Nairobi adults face a high burden of trauma, with more than half of participants showing signs of Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD) in their lifetime. The findings, shared at a dissemination event hosted by the Brain and Mind Institute (BMI) on September 24, 2025, shed light on one of Africa’s most pressing and often overlooked mental health challenges.

The study, led by Prof. Lukoye Atwoli, Deputy Director at BMI and Dean, Medical College, EA, in collaboration with international investigators Prof. Benjamin Neale and Prof. Karestan Koenen of the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health and the Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard, aimed to expand understanding of the genetic and environmental factors contributing to PTSD. The study also sought to strengthen local research capacity, reduce stigma and ensure African populations are fully represented in global psychiatric genetics research, paving the way for culturally relevant interventions and equitable mental health solutions.

Speaking at the dissemination event, Prof. Atwoli highlighted the importance of including African populations in psychiatric genetics research and the opportunities the study creates for locally relevant solutions. “Africa has historically been left behind in psychiatric genetics research, and this study marks a turning point. By focusing on African populations, we are revealing the true scale of PTSD and related disorders while generating knowledge that will lead to equitable, effective and locally relevant interventions.”

The study’s preliminary results reveal the significant burden of trauma among Kenyan adults, highlighting both the scale of PTSD and disparities across gender and geographic areas. These findings provide critical insights that can inform interventions, policy and support services for affected communities.

Key findings include:
• 55 percent of Kenyan adults are likely to have experienced PTSD in their lifetime
• 21 percent showed symptoms in the past month
• Women were disproportionately affected, with 61 percent reporting lifetime PTSD compared to 39 percent of men
• Geographic differences were recorded, with Westlands Subcounty showing the highest prevalence of PTSD symptoms in the past month at 48 percent, while Kibra recorded the lowest at 17 percent

Given the national implications of these findings, Dr. Mercy Karanja, Director of the Mental Health Division at the Ministry of Health, emphasized the importance of using this evidence to inform policy and improve access to mental health care. “These findings show us the extent to which trauma and PTSD are affecting Kenyans and remind us that mental health must be at the centre of our health priorities. With this evidence, we can design stronger policies, allocate resources more effectively and ensure communities across the country have access to care that meets their needs.”

The study also carries global significance, shedding light on the representation of African populations in psychiatric genetics. Co-investigator of the study, Dr. Sarah Kiburi, noted that the research provides an important contribution to making global mental health research more inclusive and representative.

“This is the first genome-wide study of PTSD in African ancestry populations conducted at this scale. The findings give us a clearer picture of both the genetic and environmental factors shaping mental health in Africa, and they will make global psychiatric research far more inclusive and representative, ” said Dr Kiburi.
In addition to generating knowledge, the study explored innovative approaches to care, including the STAIR Coach mobile app, which has demonstrated feasibility as a scalable tool for trauma support. The app offers accessible, practical support for individuals affected by trauma, translating research findings into real-world solutions.

Beyond this, the study has laid the groundwork for future breakthroughs by expanding into NeuroGAP Psychosis II at Mathari Hospital, furthering research into conditions such as schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, and psychosis. These efforts underscore the urgent need to prioritize mental health as an integral part of public health.
